title: Research finds family of critically ill cancer patients face anxiety and depression
content: When cancer patients reach intensive care, doctors concentrate on saving lives, yet research shows that family members, partners and friends bear a heavy burden. The study finds widespread anxiety, depression, exhaustion and declining well‑being among those supporting a loved one through a critical illness.
summary: Doctors are working to save the lives of cancer patients in intensive care. Research shows family members, partners and friends of these patients experience widespread anxiety, depression, exhaustion and declining well‑being.

title: First responders' brain injury care guidelines released with 28 recommendations
content:
Over 50 experts—clinicians, researchers, policymakers, first responders and representatives from agencies that employ and advocate for them—have reached consensus on the first recommendations for the recognition, diagnosis and management of traumatic brain injury in first responders.  

Publishing today (Oct. 16, 2026) in The Journal of Head Trauma Rehabilitation, the 52 authors agreed to 28 recommendations designed to help first responders, health‑care professionals and agencies work toward five primary goals: timely recognition of traumatic brain injury (TBI), safe recovery, operational readiness, reduced stigma and first‑responder–centered care.

title: Limited‑English new moms less likely to receive standard headache treatment after epidural
content:
A study presented at the Anesthesiology 2026 annual meeting found that new mothers with limited English proficiency are less likely to receive the standard treatment for post‑epidural headaches.  

These headaches are painful and debilitating and can occur when the membrane surrounding the spinal cord is accidentally punctured during an epidural for childbirth.
summary: New mothers with limited English proficiency are less likely to receive the standard treatment for painful and debilitating headaches that can occur if the membrane surrounding the spinal cord is accidentally punctured during an epidural for childbirth. The finding was reported in a study presented at the Anesthesiology 2026 annual meeting.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Martin explains consumer rights and cancellation options for auto‑renew subscriptions
content: Martin offered listeners guidance on dealing with auto‑renewing subscriptions, outlining the consumer rights that apply and describing how a renewal can be challenged or cancelled. His advice aims to help those who feel caught out by recurring charges.
summary: Martin provides advice for listeners caught out by auto‑renewing subscriptions. He explains the rights consumers have and whether there is a way to challenge the renewal or cancel.
author: BBC Business

title: Climate change costs remain ambiguous as impacts on extreme weather are hard to measure
content: Human activity has raised global temperatures, but quantifying the direct costs of climate change remains difficult. The impact on extreme weather—such as hurricanes and heat waves—varies locally, and both observations and climate models may fail to capture these effects accurately.
summary: Human activity has raised global temperatures, making it difficult to determine the direct costs of climate change. Impacts on extreme weather such as hurricanes and heat waves are locally specific and variable, and observations and climate models may not fully capture them.
author: Phys.org

title: Australian scavengers approach carcasses like a buffet, not just eat and leave
content:
Scientists often picture scavengers as animals that sniff out a carcass, eat rapidly and then slink away.  

Observations of Australian scavengers contradict that image; they are reported to treat a carcass more like a buffet rather than a quick meal.
summary: Australian scavengers do not simply eat everything and slink away from a carcass. Instead, they approach a carcass as if it were a buffet.
author: Phys.org

title: Salt crystals from Enceladus jets may reveal clues to subsurface ocean life
content: Salt crystals ejected from Saturn’s moon Enceladus may contain evidence of life in its subsurface ocean. Jets near the moon’s south pole spew water vapor and icy particles from the ocean beneath kilometers of ice, allowing scientists to study the hidden water without drilling.
summary: Salt crystals from Enceladus's south‑pole jets could provide clues to possible life in its hidden ocean. The ocean lies beneath kilometers of ice, but water vapor and icy particles ejected by the jets reach the surface, allowing study without drilling.
author: Phys.org

title: Hand‑cranked device determines blood type and hematocrit in one minute
content:
A newly unveiled hand‑cranked device can determine a patient’s blood type and hematocrit level in just one minute. The rapid test aims to give doctors immediate information needed for safe transfusions and to assess blood loss or anemia when injuries are severe.  

Current hospital equipment for these measurements relies on large, electricity‑powered machines and trained personnel, resources that are often missing from ambulances, disaster zones and remote clinics. The portable, manual system could fill that gap by providing critical data without power or specialist staff.
summary: The device can identify a patient’s blood type and red‑cell level within about a minute. It offers a portable alternative to large electric machines that require trained staff, which are often lacking in ambulances, disaster zones or remote clinics.
author: Phys.org

title: Quantum magic state cleanup reduces errors 40‑fold in first hardware test
content: A hardware test of a new quantum “magic state cleanup” technique cut qubit errors by a factor of 40, marking the first successful demonstration of the method. The result addresses the fragility of qubits that hampers reliable quantum computing, offering a less resource‑intensive alternative to traditional magic‑state distillation, which filters flaws but demands extensive overhead.
summary: The new quantum magic state cleanup technique cut errors by a factor of 40 in its first successful hardware test. Qubits are fragile and prone to errors, making reliable quantum computers difficult, and traditional magic state distillation filters flaws but is extremely resource‑intensive.
author: Phys.org

title: LLNL builds 3D simulations to test nuclear asteroid deflection
content:
Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory researchers are developing three‑dimensional simulations to assess how a nuclear device could deflect or potentially disrupt an asteroid threatening Earth.  

The simulations aim to evaluate mitigation options for planetary defense.
summary: Lawrence Livermore National Laboratory researchers are developing three‑dimensional simulations. The simulations examine how a nuclear device could deflect or disrupt an asteroid threatening Earth.
author: Phys.org

title: Lund University study finds complex population impact after Kikai‑Akahoya eruption
content: An international research team headed by Lund University has investigated how the prehistoric Kikai‑Akahoya volcanic eruption impacted population levels in Japan. The study’s findings, published in Science Advances, suggest that the demographic effects were more nuanced than earlier assumptions indicated. The results revise the understanding of this major volcanic disaster’s societal consequences.
summary: An international study led by Lund University examined population levels after the Kikai‑Akahoya volcanic eruption in prehistoric Japan. The researchers say the results show a more complex picture than previously believed, and the paper appears in Science Advances.
author: Phys.org

title: 1960 scientists' prediction of humanity's brink on Nov 13 2026 proves inaccurate
content:
In 1960, scientists warned that runaway population growth would push humanity to the brink of destruction on November 13, 2026, and their mathematical forecasts appeared to track reality for decades.  

Subsequent declines in birth rates and a slowdown in population growth have undermined the doomsday scenario, illustrating how even convincing scientific models can falter when human behavior shifts.
summary: In 1960 scientists predicted that runaway population growth would bring humanity to the brink of destruction on November 13, 2026, and their mathematical forecasts remained surprisingly accurate for decades. Later declines in birth rates and slower population growth caused the prediction to unravel, showing that scientific models can fail when human behavior changes.
author: Science Daily

title: Archaeologists uncover 1,200‑year‑old hairless dog mummies at Wari site in Peru
content:
Archaeologists have uncovered 1,200‑year‑old remains of Peru’s famed hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site.  

The find includes remarkably preserved mummies and puppies interred with humans; analysis of their unusual teeth, diets and burial arrangements provides new insight into how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred and sometimes discarded these animals.
summary: Archaeologists have discovered 1,200‑year‑old remains of Peru’s hairless dogs at an ancient Wari Empire burial site. The find includes remarkably preserved mummies and puppies buried alongside humans, and their unusual teeth, diets and burial arrangements reveal clues about how ancient Peruvians cared for, bred and sometimes discarded their dogs.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists discover youth protein that rejuvenates aging brain immune cells in mice
content:
Scientists discovered a youth‑associated protein that protects the brain’s immune cells from age‑related decline.  

Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ ability to clear debris and reduced signs of inflammation, raising hopes for future treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
summary: Scientists discovered a youth‑linked protein that protects the brain’s immune cells from age‑related decline. Restoring the protein in older mice improved the cells’ debris‑clearing ability and reduced inflammation, suggesting potential for treatments targeting brain aging and Alzheimer’s disease.
author: Science Daily

title: Two supermassive black holes in galaxy Mrk 501 may merge within 100 years
content:
Astronomers have uncovered compelling evidence that two supermassive black holes are spiraling toward a potentially spectacular collision at the center of galaxy Mrk 501. A previously unseen jet of particles revealed the likely presence of a second black hole, confirming the binary nature of the system.

Observations indicate the pair completes an orbit every 121 days, and, depending on their masses, the two cosmic giants could merge in as little as 100 years.
summary: Astronomers have found evidence of two supermassive black holes spiraling toward a collision at the center of galaxy Mrk 501. A newly detected particle jet suggests a second black hole, with the pair completing a 121‑day orbit and possibly merging in as little as 100 years.
author: Science Daily

title: New drug reverses severe fatty liver disease in animals by repairing gut
content: Scientists have discovered a potential new drug that reverses severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and preventing harmful substances from reaching the liver. The finding may open pathways for treatments of liver disease and other serious conditions such as cardiovascular disease.
summary: Scientists discovered a potential new drug can reverse severe fatty liver disease in animal models by restoring gut health and blocking harmful substances from reaching the liver. The breakthrough could pave the way for new treatments for liver disease and potentially other serious conditions, including cardiovascular disease.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find many sweeteners disrupt gut bacteria, especially with antidepressant
content: Scientists tested 39 sweeteners and found that many common varieties can interfere with gut bacteria. In laboratory experiments, a mixture of one sweetener with a widely prescribed antidepressant markedly reduced beneficial bacteria and overall microbial diversity, prompting new questions about possible impacts on gut health and immunity.
summary: Scientists discovered that many common sweeteners can interfere with gut bacteria, and some combinations with medications produce strong effects. In laboratory experiments, one sweetener mixed with a widely prescribed antidepressant reduced beneficial bacteria and microbial diversity, raising questions about gut health and immunity.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find deep sleep links growth hormone to muscle gain, fat loss, and brain boost
content:
Scientists discovered a two‑way relationship between sleep and growth hormone, showing deep sleep builds muscle, burns fat and boosts brain function.  

The research indicates the brain balances physical recovery with wakefulness, explaining how inadequate sleep harms metabolism and brain health and may pave the way for treatments targeting sleep and neurological disorders.
summary: Scientists discovered a two‑way relationship between sleep and growth hormone that shows the brain balances physical recovery with wakefulness. The findings may explain why poor sleep harms metabolism and brain health and could lead to new treatments for sleep and neurological disorders.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists find female mouse skin cells coordinate, male cells act independently
content:
Scientists have uncovered a surprising difference in how male and female skin repairs and renews itself. By tracking individual skin stem cells in living mice for five months, researchers observed distinct patterns of cellular behavior between the sexes.

Female skin stem cells were found to work together in a highly coordinated manner, whereas male cells operated more independently. The synchronization, driven by sex hormones, appears to explain why wounds heal faster in female mice, particularly during the first few days after injury.
summary: Researchers tracked individual skin stem cells in living mice for five months and observed that female cells work together in a highly coordinated way while male cells operate more independently. This hormone-driven synchronization helps explain why wounds heal faster in female mice, especially during the first few days.
author: Science Daily

content:

title: Meta deletes AI training clause that implied scraping of news sites
content:
Meta is revising its commercial terms after criticism, deleting language that implied the company could scrape content from websites—including news sites—to train its artificial‑intelligence systems. The change follows a backlash over the previous wording.

The removed clause stated that “Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.” Many, including Neiman Lab and James Grimmelmann, a professor of digital and information law at Cornell, interpreted it as an …
summary: After backlash, Meta is updating its terms again to remove language that suggested it could scrape content from sites, including news sites, to train its AI. Specifically, the following language no longer appears on the commercial terms page : … Meta may use any content from such domains, web pages, or URLs to provide, develop, improve, research, train, and maintain the integrity of, the Meta Company Products, services, and features provided under these Commercial Terms and any other applicable supplemental terms.
author: The Verge

title: Independent arcades see resurgence as players shift from sprawling “forever games”
content:
A semi‑nostalgic movement is emerging in the gaming world as players turn back to more focused, social experiences, prompting speculation that a new wave of independent arcades could revive the communal side of gaming. The shift follows a five‑year period during which major publishers poured hundreds of millions of dollars into “forever games” such as Fortnite, Minecraft and Roblox, creating sprawling franchises built around endless updates and battle‑pass systems.

Industry observers note that this emphasis on perpetual content has produced notable failures, including titles like Concord, Mindseye and Tales of the Shire. Even well‑received releases such as Crimson Desert, Path of Exile 2 and Blood of the Dawnwalker are described as overly bloated, consuming large portions of players’ limited free time. The growing discontent with these expansive models is fueling interest in smaller, arcade‑style venues that prioritize direct, social play.
summary: After years of sprawling ‘forever’ games, players are rediscovering the pleasures of more focused experiences. Could a new wave of independent arcades bring back the social side of gaming?
author: Guardian Technology

title: Saturday quiz asks which coffee chain was founded in London in 1971
content:
Saturday Quiz Highlights a 1971 London Coffee Chain

The Saturday quiz, titled “Which coffee chain was founded in London in 1971? The Saturday quiz,” opens with a question asking participants to name the coffee chain that began operations in London in 1971. The quiz then moves through a series of other inquiries, including a classic of political theory dedicated to Lorenzo de Medici, the only jazz act to win the Mercury Music prize, and the African country where Spanish is an official language.  

Additional questions cover a 2026 release described as the most expensive entertainment product ever created, a West Sussex estate pioneering rewilding, a gas named from the Greek for “lazy,” and the pseudonym of US doctor Sara Cohen. The quiz also references figures such as Divine, Frank Fiegel, Helen Kane, and various sports and cultural personalities.
summary: The Saturday quiz includes a question asking which coffee chain was founded in London in 1971. The quiz also contains a range of other trivia questions on topics such as political theory, music awards, languages, rewilding estates, gases and pseudonyms.

title: Apple AirPods 5 reviewed as best open‑fit earbuds with upgraded ANC
content:
Apple has unveiled the AirPods 5, positioning them as the best open‑fit earbuds yet. The new model keeps the familiar design of the popular AirPods 4 but removes silicone ear tips, offering a noise‑cancelling experience that rivals many plugged‑in designs at a lower price.

The AirPods 5 come in two versions—one with a wireless charging case and swipe controls, the other without. Prices start at £119 (€149/$129/A$219), £10 cheaper than the launch price of their predecessors. Connectivity is handled by Bluetooth 5.3, SBC, AAC, and the new H2 chip. Battery life is four to five hours with ANC, extending to 22 hours with the case. The earbuds are water‑resistant (IP57, up to 1 metre for 30 minutes) and weigh 4.3 g each.

The charging case measures 46.2 × 50.1 × 21.2 mm and weighs 32.3 g (wireless) or 34.7 g (wired). It can be charged via USB‑C or wirelessly using Qi or Apple Watch charging standards.
summary: Apple’s AirPods 5 keep the AirPods 4 design but omit silicone tips and add upgraded active‑noise cancelling that rivals many plugged‑in earbuds. They are sold with or without a wireless‑charging case, start at £119 (about $129), and deliver four to five hours of use with ANC and up to 22 hours total from the case.
author: Guardian Technology

title: AI Threat: Lack of Public Voice Fuels Resistance Against Tech-White House Alliance
content:
The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it,” writes Peter Lewis. He argues that tech bros and their highly paid sock puppets bank on society accepting an inevitability doctrine, presenting progress as a fait accompli that removes citizens from the decision‑making game. The article contends that this sense of inevitability fuels a populist wave.

Lewis notes that resistance is rising in Australia and around the world. He contrasts the United States, which still claims to be the oldest constitutional democracy, with an unholy alliance between tech overlords and the White House that is creating an AI reality untethered to the will of the people.
summary: Tech bros and their paid sock puppets rely on an inevitability doctrine that erodes public agency. In Australia and worldwide, resistance grows as the tech overlords and the White House forge an AI reality detached from the people's will.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Meta scales back AI-driven staff cuts after workers spent time fixing errors
content:
Rapid AI adoption has left workers cleaning up a flood of errors and low‑quality work, employers around the globe are grappling with the fallout, Reuters reported. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and deploy more AI agents after the company discovered employees were spending increasing time fixing technical and security errors.

In a separate move, after thinning its workforce—especially middle managers—in a 2023 efficiency push, Meta is expanding its managerial ranks again, LinkedIn posts from workers show.
summary: Employers worldwide are grappling with fallout from rapid AI adoption that left workers cleaning up technical and security errors. Meta has scaled back plans to axe staff and use more AI agents and is expanding its managerial ranks after a 2023 efficiency-driven workforce reduction, according to Reuters and LinkedIn posts.

content:

title: Huge smoke and flames over St Petersburg after large Ukrainian drone attack
content:
Huge plumes of black smoke billowed over St Petersburg, Russia’s second‑largest city, on Sunday, 18 October, as a large‑scale Ukrainian drone attack sparked fires at industrial and logistics facilities.  

Russian officials said 126 drones had been intercepted in the surrounding region.
summary: On Sunday, 18 October, huge plumes of black smoke rose over St Petersburg after a large‑scale Ukrainian drone attack set fire to industrial and logistics facilities. Russian officials said 126 drones were intercepted in the surrounding region.

title: PSG regain Ligue 1 lead after comeback win over Strasbourg
content:
PSG reclaimed the Ligue 1 lead after a dramatic comeback against Strasbourg, overturning a deficit that had persisted for over 60 minutes. The Parisians relied on their substitutes to secure the turnaround.  

The win follows PSG’s spectacular Champions League triumph over Manchester City and comes as the club prepares to face FC Barcelona, with confidence at an all‑time high.
summary: PSG trailed Strasbourg for more than 60 minutes before substitutes helped them turn the game around. The win puts PSG back on top of Ligue 1 and follows their Champions League victory over Manchester City ahead of a clash with Barcelona.

title: Paris police report record 855 arrests in protest violence, 500+ detained
content: Police in Paris announced on Sunday that they had arrested a record 855 people for protest‑related violence the day before. The prosecutor’s office said more than 500 of those individuals were being held in custody, according to France 24 analyst Shirli Sitbon.
summary: Police in Paris said Sunday they had arrested a "record" 855 people over protest-related violence in the capital the day before. The prosecutor's office said more than 500 of those arrested were being held in custody.

title: Violence erupts at France's Saturday protests, ~400 arrested, TV2 investigates perpetrators
content: Violent clashes, fires, vandalism and looting marred demonstrations across France on Saturday as hundreds of thousands marched against the rising cost of living and poor conditions in schools. The French Interior Ministry said about 400 people were arrested nationwide, and partner TV station France 2 examined who was involved in the violence.
summary: Violent clashes, fires, vandalism and looting marred demonstrations across France on Saturday as hundreds of thousands marched against the rising cost of living and poor school conditions. The French Interior Ministry said about 400 people were arrested nationwide, and France 2 examined who was involved in the violence.

title: Youth activists and Yellow Vests join Oct. 17 France protests over cost of living
content:
Saturday’s nationwide demonstration on October 17 gathered youth activists and supporters of the Yellow Vest movement in France. The rally followed weeks of student protests over poor conditions in schools and rising anger about the cost of living.  

The protesters’ primary grievance was the cost of living, and, as France 24’s Shirli Sitbon notes, they did not achieve what they wanted.
summary: Weeks of student protests over poor school conditions and rising anger over the cost of living led to a nationwide demonstration on October 17. The rally brought together youth activists and Yellow Vest supporters, but the protesters did not achieve their demands, according to France 24's Shirli Sitbon.
author: France 24

title: 800,000 join largely peaceful nationwide protests across France
content:
Protesters across France said the demonstrations “brought the entire population together for a common purpose,” as roughly 800,000 people took to the streets this weekend in cities nationwide. The largely peaceful rallies included high‑school students, railway workers and members of the Yellow Vest movement.

The unrest began after a month of student protests over educational inequality and deteriorating school facilities, then broadened into a wider outcry over the cost of living, public‑spending cuts and perceived climate‑action failures, with participants saying they have reached their breaking point.
summary: This weekend, in cities across France, some 800,000 protesters, including students, railway workers and members of the Yellow Vest movement, took to the streets in largely peaceful nationwide demonstrations. Sparked by a month of high school student protests over educational inequality and crumbling school facilities, the movement has grown into a broader outcry over the cost of living, public spending and climate inaction, as people across France say they have reached their breaking point.
author: France 24

title: Conservation groups rescue at least 51 orangutans from Indonesian wildfires
content: Dozens of critically endangered orangutans were rescued in Indonesia as rampant wildfires and a prolonged pollution spell threatened their forest habitat. Conservation groups saved at least 51 individuals between August 6 and October 19, intervening to protect the primates from the environmental crisis.
summary: Conservation groups saved at least 51 orangutans in Indonesia between August 6 and October 19. The rescues came as rampant wildfires and a months‑long pollution spell threatened the animals’ natural habitat.

title: Musk, Trump and Rubio give different answers on who capped Starlink in Ukraine
content:
Ukraine says speed limits on Starlink are still hampering its military efforts to counter Russian drones, after a surprise network slowdown that Kyiv called deliberate. Washington denied ordering the slowdown.

Musk, Trump and Rubio each gave different answers about who capped Starlink in Ukraine.
summary: Musk, Trump and Rubio each offered a different answer to who capped Starlink in Ukraine. Ukraine says speed limits on Starlink are still hampering its military's effort to counter Russian drones after a surprise slowdown that Kyiv called deliberate and Washington denied ordering.
author: France 24

title: Gaza families use flour sacks as flood barriers amid winter shelter crisis
content:
Residents in Gaza, including Ahmed Al-Omari, are bracing for another winter of bitter cold, rain and flooding, turning flour sacks into makeshift flood barriers.  

Families are surviving in tattered tents and damaged buildings as the war‑ravaged strip endures the harsh season.
summary: Families in the Gaza Strip are using flour sacks as makeshift flood barriers. Ahmed Al-Omari is preparing for another winter of bitter cold and rain that threatens flooding as families live in tattered tents and damaged buildings.

title: UN Secretary-General urges end to “war on nature” as leaders meet in Yerevan
content: The UN Secretary‑General has urged an end to the “war on nature” as governments convene in Yerevan, Armenia on Monday. Delegates will face a practical test of whether their actions are sufficient to secure peace and realign the world’s biodiversity goals with the plan outlined at COP17.
summary: The UN Secretary-General has called for an end to the “war on nature”. On Monday, governments gathering in Yerevan, Armenia will have to confront whether they are doing enough to put the world’s biodiversity goals back on track.
author: UN News

title: Michael Gove explains his support for austerity on Radical Thinking podcast
content:
Michael Gove, a veteran of British Conservatism who has served as a journalist, government minister and now editor of the Spectator, appeared on the latest episode of the podcast Radical Thinking to explain his political outlook.  In the interview with host Aditya Chakrabortty, Gove addressed the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the magazine’s position on Islam.  The full conversation is available for viewing online.

The discussion highlighted Gove’s view that austerity is “inevitably painful,” a stance he defended while reflecting on his three‑decade career shaping the Conservative agenda.  Chakrabortty pressed Gove on how his policies have evolved as the party moved further rightward, and the pair examined the implications of recent Brexit outcomes.

The episode also referenced a range of related reading, including Gove’s 1998 essay in The Moderniser’s Dilemma: Radical Politics in the Age of Blair, Richard J Evans’s piece “The Demented Dalek” in the London Review of Books, and a Guardian column by Aditya Phil Burton‑Cartledge on the Conservative Party’s trajectory.  Additional suggested material covers topics such as the economics of the Cameron years, the impact of Brexit on UK GDP, and a recent Spectator column by Nesrine Malik critiquing the magazine’s stance on Islam.
summary: Michael Gove joins Aditya Chakrabortty on the Radical Thinking podcast to discuss the future of the right, his record on Brexit and austerity, and the Spectator’s stance on Islam. He has been a journalist, government minister and is now editor of the Spectator, a leading figure in British Conservatism for more than three decades.
author: Guardian World

title: Lisbon tent camp and Milan march protest rising costs, rioters clash with police
content:
Protests over housing and living‑cost pressures that have roiled Spain and France have spread to Italy and Portugal. In Milan, a march on Saturday to denounce rising expenses began peacefully but turned violent when masked rioters hurled stones, paving blocks and other objects at riot police and ignited barricades built from bar tables. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni described the demonstration as being exploited by “hooligans.”

In Lisbon, a tent encampment of hundreds of demonstrators was set up over the weekend, demanding action on the same issues. The camps and clashes underscore growing public frustration with housing and cost‑of‑living conditions in the two cities.
summary: Hundreds gathered in a tent encampment in Lisbon demanding action on housing and living costs. In Milan, a march against rising living costs turned violent when masked rioters threw stones and other objects at police and set fire to barricades.
author: Guardian World

title: Two dead, 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine trade strikes on power infrastructure
content:
Two people have been killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine continue to trade strikes on each other’s power infrastructure, a flare‑up that followed the breakdown of Donald Trump’s short‑lived, unilaterally declared “energy ceasefire.”  

Ukraine launched more than 1,000 drones in one of its largest aerial bombardments, targeting Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres. The overnight drone raid left one person dead and 15 wounded, contributing to the overall casualty count.
summary: Two people were killed and at least 17 injured as Russia and Ukraine exchanged attacks on power infrastructure after the breakdown of Donald Trump’s declared “energy ceasefire”. Ukraine deployed more than 1,000 drones against Russian oil depots, logistics facilities and datacentres, killing one person and wounding 15 overnight.
author: Guardian World

title: Arrests in France protests rise to 1,800 as streets in Paris devastated
content:
Arrests linked to France’s protests have risen to 1,800, with the interior minister declaring “the Republic will not yield” as whole streets in Paris are described as “devastated.” The surge in detentions comes amid what officials call the country’s worst unrest in years.

The turmoil has spread beyond France, affecting Spain and prompting similar demonstrations in Italy and Portugal. In Milan, rioters clashed with police and set property on fire, while a tent encampment appeared in Lisbon over the weekend, according to Sam Jones, reporting from Madrid.
summary: Interior minister says ‘the Republic will not yield’ to France’s worst protests in years A dispatch here from Sam Jones, our reporter in Madrid, as protests have spread to Italy and Portugal The angry protests…

title: Protected plover becomes 12th man on Windsor Park cricket ground as staff mow around nest
content:
A protected bird has become the unofficial 12th man at Windsor Park oval in Riverside, just outside Launceston, as ground staff carefully mow around its nest during weekend cricket matches.  

The resident plover – identified in reports as a masked lapwing – has claimed a spot in the middle of the community sports ground, showing no concern for the games being played nearby while it warms a nest of eggs. Locals have affectionately dubbed the bird “Faf Swoop Plessis,” a play on former South African captain Faf du Plessis.
summary: A protected masked lapwing has nested in the middle of Windsor Park oval in Riverside, near Launceston, Tasmania. Staff have been mowing around the nest while the bird, nicknamed “Faf Swoop Plessis,” remains indifferent to weekend cricket matches.
author: Guardian World

title: 13-year-old ebike rider charged with sexual touching on northern beaches
content:
A 13‑year‑old boy riding an e‑bike has been charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent after alleged harassment of females aged 13 to 54 on walking trails on Sydney’s northern beaches.  

New South Wales police said a strike force was established to investigate inappropriate comments and alleged sexual touching incidents on walking trails in the Narrabeen area during the first weeks of October, and the boy was arrested on Saturday evening.
summary: A 13-year-old boy riding an e‑bike was charged with offensive behaviour and sexual touching without consent involving females aged 13 to 54. He was arrested on Saturday evening after a police strike force investigated alleged inappropriate comments and sexual touching on walking trails in the Narrabeen area of Sydney’s northern beaches in early October.

title: Indigenous woman shackled to Queensland hospital bed during labour
content:
An advocacy group says an incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend.  

The birth occurred just days before the Labor Party and the Coalition blocked a bill that would have banned the “barbaric practice” of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth.
summary: An incarcerated Indigenous woman was shackled to a hospital bed in Queensland while she was in labour last weekend, an advocacy group said. The birth occurred days before Labor and the Coalition blocked a bill to ban the “barbaric practice” of shackling incarcerated women during childbirth.
author: Guardian World

title: Pope Leo XIV thanks well‑wishers at first event after cancer surgery
content: Pope Leo XIV thanked well‑wishers in his first public appearance since a lung‑cancer diagnosis and surgery, reciting the traditional Angelus prayer from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace. The brief ceremony marked his return to duties following the operation.
summary: Pope Leo XIV thanked well‑wishers at his first public appearance after lung cancer surgery. He recited the Angelus prayer from the balcony of the Apostolic Palace.

title: Meeting science finds bosses should speak less in meetings
content:
A growing body of research is turning the everyday ritual of meetings into a scientific discipline.  Roughly one billion meetings occur daily worldwide, and CEOs spend nearly three‑quarters of their workdays in them, according to the new overview.  Organizational and social psychologists are now mining archived virtual sessions to understand how these gatherings function and how they might be improved.

The emerging field, dubbed “meeting science,” examines gatherings of people with a goal or structure, as defined by organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology.  Kreamer co‑authored a review of more than three decades of research in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior, highlighting how meetings satisfy basic human needs to connect, communicate and cooperate.  The discipline’s rapid expansion promises clearer guidance on making meetings more purposeful and efficient.
summary: CEOs spend nearly three-quarters of their workdays in meetings, and meeting science is a growing field studying their effectiveness. Organizational psychologist Liana Kreamer of the Florida Institute of Technology coauthored a review of over three decades of meeting science in the 2026 Annual Review of Organizational Psychology and Organizational Behavior.
author: Ars Technica

title: Replit switches default model provider to OpenAI, keeping Claude available
content:
Replit announced that OpenAI will become its default model provider, replacing Anthropic.

CEO Masad clarified over the weekend that the shift makes OpenAI the default, while Anthropic’s Claude will remain accessible to customers on the platform.
summary: Over the weekend, Masad said OpenAI will replace Anthropic as Replit’s default model provider. Claude will remain available to customers on the platform.
author: TechCrunch

title: Wikipedia's 68 million articles consulted trillions of times despite trust concerns
content:
Wikipedia’s 68 million articles have been consulted trillions of times, a staggering reach for a site that has changed little since its 2001 founding by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger. The English‑language edition alone now contains 5.2 billion words, underscoring how deeply the free encyclopedia has woven itself into everyday life.

Despite that ubiquity, public perception has lingered on the “don’t trust it” refrain, rooted in the notion that anyone can edit the platform. The paradox is evident: users rely on Wikipedia so extensively that even donors attribute their contributions to “fact‑checkers,” although the site has no paid fact‑checking staff.

In an era where social‑media platforms often feel increasingly hostile, Wikipedia stands out as a digital relic that has survived largely unchanged in both function and appearance. This nostalgic holdover prompts both admiration for its endurance and concern for its fragile future.
summary: Wikipedia has 68 million articles and has been consulted trillions of times. Founded by Jimmy Wales and Larry Sanger in 2001, the site’s reputation remains challenged by perceptions that it is untrustworthy.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Tech billionaires spend over $1 million daily to oppose California’s Prop 40 billionaire tax
content:
Tech billionaires have raised more than $340 million to oppose Prop 40, a one‑time 5 % wealth tax intended to fund healthcare and education in California. State financial disclosures show the opposition campaign is spending over $1 million a day to defeat the measure as the election approaches.

During the first 19 days of September, the campaign spent at least $21.2 million, surpassing the $1‑million‑per‑day threshold. The funds are being used for a rapid‑fire outreach effort that includes robotexts, mailers and television advertisements.

Voters are receiving messages that warn a billionaire tax would “expose all Californians to higher taxes,” according to one of the ads. The intensified spending comes with less than a month left before the ballot.
summary: Tech billionaires have raised more than $340m to defeat Prop 40, a one-time 5% wealth tax that will fund healthcare and education Tech billionaires have been dumping hundreds of millions of dollars into the fight against a wealth tax in California. They’ve raised more than $340m, and the campaign they’re funding is spending more than $1m a day to defeat the measure, according to state financial disclosures.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Oscar‑tipped documentary examines the enduring fascination with Elizabeth Holmes
content:
‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth Holmes

An Oscar‑tipped documentary on the former entrepreneur‑turned‑fraudster Elizabeth Holmes has drawn fresh attention to her bizarre legacy. The film, still in development, promises an unusual look at the story that has captivated the public.

David Agus, a medical oncologist, recalls his first encounter with Holmes at a health conference. In the green room he described her as personable and pleasant, but on stage she was “a different person.” Agus noted that “the accent changed: this deep voice, very serious,” and that the transition felt as if he had met a separate individual.

Agus, speaking by phone from Los Angeles, said the shift from the green room to the stage was unprecedented for him, underscoring the enigmatic nature of Holmes that the new documentary seeks to explore.
summary: The Oscar‑tipped new documentary examines the strange legacy of entrepreneur‑turned‑fraudster Elizabeth Holmes. Medical oncologist David Agus said his first meeting with Holmes at a health conference was pleasant in the green room, but on stage she spoke with a deep, serious voice and a different accent.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Top toys and gifts for eight-year-olds, chosen by kids their own age
content:
A consumer guide of toys and gifts for eight‑year‑olds was compiled by a panel of eight‑year‑old testers. The young reviewers evaluated a range of products, from science kits and karaoke machines to shower sets and brain‑boosting games, selecting the items they enjoyed most.

The guide notes that eight‑year‑olds are developing clearer interests and skills—they are more confident readers, strategic thinkers and curious about how things work—yet still need ample playtime for wellbeing. The list highlights the most popular choices among the child testers, offering parents insight into age‑appropriate gifts.
summary: The guide lists toys and gifts such as science kits, karaoke machines, shower sets and brain‑boosting games that were tested and liked by eight‑year‑old children. It notes that eight‑year‑olds are becoming more confident readers, strategic thinkers and curious about how things work, while still needing ample play for wellbeing.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Britain urged to reject cheap, open-weight Chinese AI from DeepSeek and Xiaomi
content:
Britain is being urged to turn away from inexpensive Chinese artificial‑intelligence products, which critics say lack the security safeguards and benign intent typically built into Western technology.  

Chinese firms such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi are releasing new “open‑weight” AI models each month, allowing businesses and governments in the West to download and run the core software without paying ongoing licence fees, a practice that has sparked fears about the safety and reliability of the technology.
summary: Chinese AI developers such as DeepSeek and Xiaomi release monthly “open-weight” models that can be used without paying an ongoing licence. The article argues that the lack of security and benign intent in Chinese AI creates a risk for businesses and governments in the west.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Austrian Green MEP Lena Schilling urges EU action after nude deepfakes surface
content:
Austrian Green Party MEP Lena Schilling said she felt “disgusted” after learning that nude deepfakes of herself were circulating online and urged the European Union to act. She described the non‑consensual, digitally altered images as “digital violence against women” and a threat to democracy.

Schilling said she discovered the deepfakes last month when links led to altered photos from one of her first press conferences, with her clothing removed. A report cited in her remarks found that one in six female MEPs have been targeted by sexualised AI‑generated content.
summary: Lena Schilling of Austrian Greens says images are ‘digital violence against women’ and a threat to democracy An Austrian MEP has spoken out about her experience of being “stripped naked” online without her consent and has urged the EU to take action, as a report found that one in six female MEPs had been targeted by sexualised AI-generated content. Lena Schilling of the Green party said she had learned last month about nude deepfakes of herself circulating online.
author: Guardian Technology

title: Anthropic reports AI worm that self‑replicates across smart TVs
content:
Anthropic’s offensive research team released a report this week describing a self‑replicating “AI worm” that can spread autonomously through internet‑connected smart televisions and potentially other ordinary devices. The red‑team researchers built a malicious AI program that divided itself across 15 televisions, allowing each fragment to draw a small amount of power from its host and collectively maintain functionality.

The team noted that while AI‑driven software typically requires substantial computing resources, the worm’s design shows that capability can be distributed across low‑power devices. Anthropic warned that current trends in hardware and software could make such AI worms feasible by the end of the year, raising concerns about the ease with which future AI malware might propagate without human intervention.
summary: The tech company says successful AI worms need more capability on less powerful devices, but current trends make that feasible by the end of the year Warnings about what artificial intelligence might do in the future – together with alarming reports of what it has gotten up to already – are being issued so quickly that even security experts have difficulty triaging what to worry about. Yet a report this week from Anthropic’s offensive research team grabbed attention by describing a new, practical threat, one devoid of human characteristics or apocalyptic musings.
author: Guardian Technology

title: World Bank urges developing nations to build low‑connectivity “small AI” models
content:
The World Bank is urging developing countries to kickstart the creation of “small AI” models that can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity, to reap the full benefits of artificial intelligence. Bank’s chief knowledge officer Paschal Donohoe said the tech could speed up economic development from centuries to decades.  

He noted that while Silicon Valley big tech firms focus on ever more sophisticated consumer products, AI could accelerate development for emerging economies only if it is adapted to local needs.
summary: The World Bank is urging developing countries to create “small AI” models that can run on a mobile phone with low connectivity. Chief knowledge officer Paschal Donohoe said such AI could accelerate economic development for emerging economies if adapted to local needs.

title: Manuel’s Tavern in Atlanta Remains Political Hub as Jon Ossoff Leads Midterm Polls
content:
Manuel’s Tavern, an Atlanta landmark since its 1956 opening, has long hosted legendary Democratic leaders. Its founder helped shift the city from a Republican to a Democratic stronghold.

title: Ukrainian drone attack on Saint Petersburg kills one, injures five, sparks refinery fire
content: A large‑scale Ukrainian drone attack on Russia’s second‑largest city, Saint Petersburg, killed at least one person and hospitalised five others on Sunday. The strike also ignited fires at an oil refinery and a nearby depot. Kyiv has meanwhile accused Russia of breaching Washington’s “energy ceasefire” dozens of times.
summary: A large‑scale Ukrainian drone attack on Saint Petersburg killed at least one person and hospitalised five others on Sunday. The strike also sparked fires at an oil refinery and depot, and Kyiv accused Russia of violating Washington's "energy ceasefire" dozens of times.

title: France protests: There's a whole range of grievances at play
content:
France protests have sparked debate over the underlying causes of public anger. Experts argue the unrest may stem from either declining living standards or a perception that the economic burden is being distributed unfairly.  

In a discussion with senior lecturer Joseph Downing of Aston University, the focus was on identifying which of these grievances—economic decline or perceived inequity—is driving the current protests.
summary: The article examines whether anger in France stems from declining living standards or the perception of an unfair distribution of economic burden. It includes a discussion with Joseph Downing, senior lecturer in politics and international relations at Aston University.
author: France 24

title: France counts cost of violent protests
content: France is tallying the damage after violent protests that left the nation “like we had a war,” officials said. The unrest, which erupted on Saturday, prompted authorities to arrest 1,800 people. Demonstrators torched a historic town hall and engaged in widespread looting, leaving extensive property loss across the country.
summary: France was reeling on Sunday from widespread damage caused by violent protests. The protests the day before resulted in 1,800 arrests, a historic town hall being torched, and widespread looting.
author: France 24

title: Escalating European protests and migrant boat tragedy highlighted in images
content:

content:

title: Indonesia to drop dry ice over South Sumatra to combat fire haze
content:
Indonesia’s coordinating security minister announced that a pilot project will drop dry ice from an aircraft over South Sumatra on Thursday, marking a new tactic in the fight against the nation’s raging fires. The move follows earlier efforts that included cloud‑seeding, water‑bombing and deploying army personnel to combat the blazes.

Officials said the fires are generating a toxic haze that has spread across the region and drawn criticism from neighboring countries. The dry‑ice dispersal aims to suppress the smoke and improve air quality in the affected provinces.

title: Air Force Museum of New Zealand releases 1938 aerial photos of Nikumaroro
content:
The Air Force Museum of New Zealand has released nearly 50 black‑and‑white photographs taken during a 1938 aerial survey of Nikumaroro, the Pacific atoll believed to be where Amelia Earhart crash‑landed.

The museum published the images after a US expedition to Nikumaroro sparked renewed interest in the long‑standing mystery, providing amateur sleuths with new material to examine for possible traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane.
summary: Images from New Zealand aerial survey of Nikumaroro in 1938 offer new clues over aviator’s disappearance A New Zealand museum has released nearly 50 photos from a 1938 aerial survey of the island where Amelia Earhart is believed to have crash-landed, offering amateur sleuths new evidence to scour for traces of the pioneering aviator and her plane. content:

A local doctor reported that hospitals in Edmonton are receiving patients as Wainwright is “completely overwhelmed” by the number of injuries.

title: Argentina's president targets Falkland oil sector, warns fisheries amid renewed hostility
content:
‘4,000 people minding our own business’: four decades on, the Falkland Islands are again confronting a hostile Argentina, as the Argentine president, whose poll numbers are slipping, has turned economic pressure toward the islands’ oil sector and hinted that the lucrative fisheries industry could be the next target.

The tension was palpable inside the wood‑panelled courtroom that also serves as the Falkland Islands’ legislative assembly. A dozen local residents and a uniformed military police officer took seats at the back, while six of the eight assembly members – five men and one woman – waited at desks and microphones under a heating system set just short of uncomfortable.

Outside, the Stanley harbour churned with dark, ship‑wreck‑speckled water and strong swells, a typical blowy evening for the south Atlantic spring. Portraits of King Charles and dusty photographs of former governors lined the walls, bearing silent witness to the renewed diplomatic strain.
summary: Argentina’s president, whose poll numbers are falling, has begun economic attacks on the Falkland Islands’ oil industry. He has also suggested the islands’ key fisheries sector could be targeted next.

title: Descendant celebrates biography of Sarah Forbes Bonetta, gifted to Queen Victoria
content:
Bayo Randle, the great‑great‑grandson of Sarah Forbes Bonetta, has welcomed the publication of a new biography that chronicles his ancestor’s extraordinary journey from Africa to the British court. The book recounts how, at seven years old, she was presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a “diplomatic gift” from an African king.  

The biography details her early name, Àìná, her capture and transport to England, and Victoria’s role in funding her education, approving her marriage to one of West Africa’s wealthiest men, and serving as godmother to Bonetta’s eldest daughter.
summary: Bayo Randle’s great‑great‑grandmother was a seven‑year‑old girl named Àìná who was captured by an African king, taken to England and presented to Queen Victoria at Windsor Castle as a diplomatic gift. Victoria paid for her education, approved her marriage to one of West Africa’s wealthiest men, and became godmother to her eldest daughter.

title: Toby Shang, viral Afrobeats hypeman behind hit “Shedibalabala” and Afrohype pioneer
content:
A high‑octane, ad‑libbed style of emceeing is reshaping Afrobeats, with performers using rapid‑fire jokes and “100,000‑volt” energy to captivate audiences. The trend traces back to a 2015 freshman at the University of Lagos, whose first‑semester presentation impressed classmates so much that they nicknamed him Toby Shang, after the 16th‑century Chinese dynasty he studied.

Toby Shang’s crowd‑engagement skills stem from his high‑school experience as a ginger‑man (energiser) in a three‑person band and his work as a private tutor. By his final university year, his viral catchphrases and infectious stage presence produced the hit song “Shedibalabala.” He now describes himself as an “evangelist and pioneer” of a new Afrobeats sub‑genre that some label Afrohype or lamba.

title: Doomsday for Wallabies and Les Kiss as clinical All Blacks expose fault lines
content:
Les Kiss’s tenure as Wallabies coach has been met with severe criticism following a significant defeat to the All Blacks in the Bledisloe Cup. The loss marks Australia’s 13th consecutive loss to New Zealand and has triggered "Doomsday protocols" for the team. The match took place at Eden Park, where the Wallabies held the All Blacks to parity at half-time but ultimately conceded 26 unanswered points in the second half.

Despite the All Blacks fielding an understrength squad, the Wallabies were heavily outmatched, a result that highlights the massive gulf between the two rugby powers. This performance serves as a stark reminder of Australia’s current standing in the global rugby hierarchy. The defeat comes just one year before the teams are scheduled to meet again in Sydney during a World Cup, an event where Australia will host and must perform to maintain its status as a top-tier rugby nation.

Australia’s embarrassing capitulation to the All Blacks – their 13th in a row – is a cold reminder of where the Wallabies sit in rugby’s world order.

title: Mark Cocker Nears 1,000th Guardian Country Diary Entry
content:
Mark Cocker has reached a milestone for the world’s oldest column in an English‑language newspaper, completing his 1,000th Guardian country diary.  

His first diary, written in the autumn of 1987, described a jay burying acorns in a field near Norwich. Thirty‑nine years later, many of those acorns have grown into mature oaks.  

Cocker’s next entry will examine the changing birdlife around Flint Clough in the Peak District, a place where he first marveled at rare birds aged 12 after devouring bird books in his bedroom. As a boy he would find cuckoo, golden plover, ring ouzel and twite, a once‑common bird now virtually extinct in England.
summary: Mark Cocker is completing his 1,000th entry for the Guardian’s country diary, the world’s oldest column in an English-language newspaper, and his next diary will reflect on changing birdlife around Flint Clough. His first diary, written in 1987, described a jay burying acorns near Norwich, a scene that now reflects the mature oaks that grew from those acorns.

content:

The report found that major U.S. firms and trade associations—including Cargill, Bunge, Mondelēz, and the U.S. Soybean Export Council—along with numerous other U.S. organizations, sought to influence the EUDR in more than 350 meetings.

title: Mobile app monitoring linked to fewer post‑surgery complications, study shows
content:
Mobile app‑based monitoring may help address the vulnerable days and weeks after surgery when recovery shifts from the hospital to home with little direct supervision, a new study presented at the Anesthesiology 2026 annual meeting found.

Patients using mobile apps had a lower risk of serious complications, emergency room visits and readmissions after surgery, but the benefits depended on physician or other clinician involvement, rather than the technology alone, the researchers reported.

The study highlights that clinician involvement is key to realizing the potential benefits of mobile app monitoring for post‑surgery patients.

title: UK trial finds anesthesia choice does not affect patient recovery after major surgery
content:
A landmark trial conducted in the United Kingdom has found that the choice of general anesthetic does not impact patient recovery after major surgery. This conclusion is based on the largest-ever trial comparing the two primary anesthesia techniques utilized within the National Health Service (NHS).

The findings indicate that clinicians and patients may continue to select an anesthetic method based on individual preference rather than clinical necessity regarding recovery outcomes.
summary: The largest-ever trial in the NHS found that the choice of general anesthetic for major surgery does not affect patient recovery. Therefore, clinicians can continue to base anesthetic choice on patient and clinician preference.

title: El Niño's Weather Interplay Threatens Great Barrier Reef
content:
A strong El Niño event currently active in the Pacific Ocean is raising concerns about marine heat waves and coral bleaching that threaten Australia’s Great Barrier Reef. New research highlights how complex interactions between atmospheric patterns and weather systems located thousands of kilometers apart can combine to create conditions potentially fatal for coral reefs.

These distant weather systems appear to form a "perfect storm" that exacerbates the risks posed by the El Niño phenomenon. The study details this interplay, indicating that the convergence of these specific atmospheric factors significantly increases the threat level for the reef's ecosystem.
summary: The strong El Niño in the Pacific Ocean threatens the Great Barrier Reef with marine heat waves and coral bleaching. New research shows that distant atmospheric patterns can combine to create a potentially fatal recipe for coral reefs.

content:

The findings reveal that this trend toward reduced emotional explicitness occurs both across different generations of artists and within the individual careers of musicians.

content:

title: Hackers remotely raise temps in thousands of French supermarket freezers
content:
A large‑scale cyber‑attack hit France’s supermarket refrigeration systems shortly before midnight on Sunday, causing digital thermostats in hundreds of cold aisles to flicker and raise temperatures dramatically. The intrusion forced thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets to shift from as low as ‑27 °C (‑16.6 °F) to well over 50 °C (122 °F).

The unprecedented temperature surge left the country, described as Europe’s most hacked nation, with a significant amount of spoiled food and waste. The incident was reported as a remote override of the temperature settings, but the identity of the hackers was not disclosed.
summary: Shortly before midnight last Sunday, digital thermostats controlling hundreds of supermarket cold aisles across France began to flicker and rise. In a “bizarre and unprecedented” cyber‑attack, hackers remotely overrode temperature settings on thousands of freezers, fridges and chiller cabinets, pushing them from as low as –27 °C to over 50 °C.

title: Former national security adviser Peter Ricketts urges UK ministers to be honest on Russian threat
content:
Peter Ricketts, a former Foreign Office head and former national security adviser who advised Prime Minister David Cameron, warned that ministers must be truthful with the British public about the immediate threat posed by Russia. He said the danger could soon result in loss of life.

Ricketts called for greater resilience in protecting the United Kingdom’s banking, energy and water systems against cyber‑assaults. He highlighted the scale of “hybrid attacks” being directed by Vladimir Putin’s forces.

The former adviser’s comments add to a growing chorus of officials urging the government to acknowledge and address the Russian threat.
summary: Peter Ricketts, a former national security adviser who advised David Cameron, said ministers must be honest with the British public about the immediate threat from Russia. title: Senior Labour figures warn AI power could outpace public and pose safety risks
content:
Westminster is increasingly alert to warnings over artificial‑intelligence safety, with senior Labour figures expressing concern about the technology’s power and the risk of “falling behind the public.”  The party’s leaders are also uneasy about AI’s potential use by extremist groups and other bad actors.

At the Labour conference, a cabinet minister warned, “I have this sense that, within a few months, AI is going to be all anyone is talking about,” highlighting the speed of the issue’s rise.  The remarks came as ministers and activists celebrated Andy Burnham’s recent takeover and a poll bounce following the change of leader.

title: Writer Linda Geddes uncovers fraudster who stole her byline on New York Post article
content:
Writer Linda Geddes discovered that her byline had been fraudulently attached to a New York Post article on “chronoworking.” The misuse came to light after a LinkedIn user tagged her in a post praising the piece, prompting Geddes to click the link and find her name listed above an article about people who organize their work around biological clocks.

Geddes, the author of a book on circadian rhythms, said she had never heard of the person who posted the comment, nor had she written or interviewed anyone for the article. The incident has led her to investigate the identity of the impersonator and the source of the false attribution.
summary: Linda Geddes was tagged in a LinkedIn post claiming she contributed to a New York Post piece on “chronoworking.” She found her name listed as the author of the article despite never having written or interviewed for it.

title: Palantir patient data tech rejected by many NHS trusts in England
content:
NHS organisations across England are rejecting Palantir’s patient‑data technology, according to freedom‑of‑information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases.

Some health bodies reported that the £330 million federated data platform (FDP) operated by the controversial US company had made it easier to manage waiting lists and had improved surgery scheduling. However, from Gateshead to Truro, other trusts said they declined to use the platform or had carried out trials and reverted to older systems.

A Suffolk trust said other systems “supercede” the FDP’s functionality, while Greater Manchester’s care board called the Palantir system “duplicative” and “retrograde”. The decision reflects differing assessments of the platform’s value across NHS trusts.
summary: Exclusive: health bodies across country say controversial US firm’s data platform no better than systems already in useNHS organisations that care for millions of people in England are rejecting Palantir’s patient data technology, according to freedom of information responses that reveal health bosses believe they can find better or equal alternatives in many cases. title: Kenya reports third Ebola case, contact tracing continues
content:
Kenya’s health ministry has confirmed a third Ebola case, identifying a 65‑year‑old woman—related to a man who died earlier this month after traveling from the Democratic Republic of the Congo—as testing positive while in quarantine.

The woman had been in quarantine since 5 October, and a second patient, a 39‑year‑old man from the same family, remains in stable condition. Officials say there is no evidence of community transmission because both individuals were under quarantine.

Three contacts have yet to be traced, and the health ministry continues contact‑tracing efforts, according to correspondent Bastien Renouil.

title: Uganda Begins Phase 1 Ebola Vaccine Trial in Masaka
content:
Uganda has begun a Phase 1 trial of a vaccine candidate targeting the Bundibugyo strain of the Ebola virus. The study is taking place in the town of Masaka, located in southern Uganda, where the virus is currently circulating.

The trial focuses on a vaccine designed specifically for the Bundibugyo strain, for which no approved treatment or vaccine exists. Researchers are evaluating the safety and initial efficacy of the candidate in this early-stage study.

content:

The attack occurred as gunmen opened fire on mourners attending a wake, killing a young woman in the same incident.  

The shooting has revived concerns about the safety of journalists in Cameroon’s English‑speaking regions, where years of conflict between government forces and separatist groups have persisted.

content:

title: James McClean says wearing the poppy was never an option
content:

McClean described how people see him as “a madman” and “a loudmouth,” but he says the reality is the opposite: “I’m pretty boring. I go training, go home and switch off.” He spent 14 years in English football, played 103 times for Ireland, and appeared in 150 Premier League games over five seasons. In total he has played 800 professional games and earned a number of individual accolades.

Despite being at war with his club, Derry City, McClean remains the only footballer from the north of Ireland to win over 100 caps for the Republic of Ireland. He counts his achievements as success and says he has no regrets.

title: Chris Woakes says curfew ruined England's World Cup celebration
content:
Chris Woakes, in an extract from his new book, recalls the day England won the 2019 Cricket World Cup. He describes the atmosphere at Lord’s, where the stadium was packed to the rafters and the celebrations were in full flow, complete with fireworks and ticker‑tape.

On the podium, Woakes says he felt a mix of pride and relief, laughing with his old mate Mark Wood. He notes that Wood was standing next to Jason Roy in the lineup, and that he grabbed a fistful of Roy’s shirt, pulling it up while they jumped around like lunatics.

Woakes also mentions that, at the pinnacle of his career, Roy was battling to stop his gut from hanging out, a detail he shares to illustrate the intensity of the moment.
summary: In his new book, England bowler Chris Woakes recalls the team's celebration after winning the World Cup and the curfew imposed by the ECB. He describes the packed Lord's stadium, fireworks, and the team's resentment as the ECB curfew ended the party.

title: Houthi missile threats delay Saudi football match
content:
Houthi conflict casts shadow as Saudi Arabia scales back sporting pipe dreams. A match in the Asian Champions League Elite was delayed by missile‑attack warnings, underscoring the impact of Yemen’s Houthi rebels on the kingdom’s sporting calendar.

The game on Monday night saw Al‑Nassr defeat Uzbek side Neftchi Fergana 3‑1. The Saudi club, coached by Ange Postecoglou, earned the win with goals from Cristiano Ronaldo and Sadio Mané. Ronaldo also grabbed a scarf in the colours of the Saudi flag and waved it to a sparse but enthusiastic crowd that responded with rapturous cheers.

A safety warning was issued 15 minutes before kick‑off, two days after Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid International Airport killed 13 people and wounded more than 300. The threat of missile attacks and the resulting delay highlighted the challenges facing Saudi Arabia’s ambition to host high‑profile sporting events.
summary: The match between Al‑Nassr and Neftchi Fergana was delayed by a missile attack warning from Yemen’s Houthi rebels. Al‑Nassr won 3‑1, with Cristiano Ronaldo and Sadio Mané scoring, while the game saw low attendance and safety concerns after Houthi strikes on Riyadh’s King Khalid airport.

content:

The loss, described as a “second thrashing in a week,” saw New Zealand dominate at the breakdown, moving the ball forward with little resistance and limiting the Wallabies to just three attacking forays amid errors and execution failures. Concerns are mounting for Les Kiss’s side as the World Cup approaches.

title: Optical imaging links altered metabolism and oxygen use in Alzheimer's disease
content:
Optical imaging techniques have revealed a connection between altered metabolism and oxygen utilization in Alzheimer's disease. While the disorder is widely recognized for impairing memory and cognition, researchers note that it also disrupts how brain cells generate and consume energy.

Mitochondria, the cellular structures that provide most of a cell’s energy, can become dysfunctional in the disease. Concurrently, changes in cerebral blood flow and oxygen availability may increase metabolic demands on brain tissue. Understanding the interaction of these factors could aid scientists in characterizing the metabolic changes that accompany Alzheimer’s disease.
summary: Alzheimer's disease involves changes in brain cell energy production and use, including mitochondrial dysfunction and altered blood flow and oxygen availability. Optical imaging links these altered metabolism and oxygen use, aiding researchers in characterizing disease-related metabolic changes.

content:

title: Brain PET scans aid selection and monitoring of patients for new Alzheimer's drugs
content:
Brain PET scans are increasingly used to select and monitor patients receiving new Alzheimer’s disease therapies, according to recent reports on nuclear medicine advances.  

Amyloid PET imaging is employed to confirm the presence of amyloid pathology, helping clinicians decide whether to prescribe anti‑amyloid drugs. In addition, tau PET scans are used to supply further information on disease progression and prognosis.  

These imaging tools enable clinicians to visualize the biological changes associated with Alzheimer’s disease and guide treatment decisions for patients undergoing novel therapies.
summary: Nuclear medicine, including brain PET scans, is increasingly used to visualize biological changes in Alzheimer's disease and guide treatment decisions. Amyloid PET imaging confirms amyloid pathology for patients on anti‑amyloid drugs, and tau PET scans add information on disease progression and prognosis.
author: Medical Xpress

title: South London study finds ethnic stroke disparities stem from risk factor differences
content:
A new south London study conducted at King’s College London found that ethnic disparities in stroke incidence are largely explained by differences in traditional stroke risk factors rather than ethnicity itself.  

The research identified conditions such as diabetes and high blood pressure as the primary contributors to stroke risk across ethnic groups. Consequently, the study suggests that addressing these modifiable risk factors could reduce the observed inequalities in stroke outcomes.
summary: A new south London study conducted at King's College London found that stroke risk is primarily linked to traditional risk factors such as diabetes and high blood pressure. The researchers concluded that these risk‑factor differences, rather than ethnicity, explain ethnic inequalities in stroke.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study: Justifying political violence increases voter approval, among BJP supporters
content:
A study published in The Journal of Politics examines how framing political violence as a justified response to an out‑group threat or injustice affects voter attitudes. The research was conducted by Ursula Daxecker, director at the Max Planck Institute for Politics and Social Science in Göttingen, and Neeraj Prasad of the University of Amsterdam.

The authors find that presenting violence as legitimate increases public approval not only of the violent acts themselves but also of the political parties that employ them. The effect is especially pronounced among supporters of India’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), who, when exposed to justifications for violence, show reduced approval of a peaceful response offered by their own party.
summary: The study by Ursula Daxecker, director at the Max Planck Institute for Politics and Social Science in Göttingen, and Neeraj Prasad of the University of Amsterdam, published in The Journal of Politics, finds that legitimizing political violence can increase public approval of both the violence and the parties involved. Among BJP supporters, the effect was stronger, with justified violence reducing their approval of a peaceful response by their own party.
author: Phys.org

title: Naming a chicken reduces preschoolers' poultry selection, study finds
content:
A new paper by researchers from SWPS University finds that giving a chicken a name and describing its favorite habits can reduce preschoolers’ selection of poultry. The study shows that this brief identification leads children to choose poultry less often, influencing both their verbal statements and actual meal choices.  

Despite the empathy effect, the researchers note that children’s pre‑existing food preferences still most often dominate their decisions, outweighing the impact of animal identifiability. The results were reported in the university’s recent publication.
summary: Naming a chicken and describing its favorite habits leads preschoolers to choose poultry less often. The effect shows up in verbal declarations and actual meal choices, but food preferences usually outweigh empathy, according to a new paper by researchers from SWPS University.

title: Fakeipedia launches as AI-powered wiki for fictional worlds
content:
Show HN: Fakeipedia – Wikipedia for worlds that don't exist

Fakeipedia is an automatic world‑building platform that generates a complete wiki for an imagined world, allowing users to explore it endlessly by clicking red links. The author, who developed the idea after experimenting with worldbuilding in Gemini, waited until a powerful enough model could produce quality content before releasing the project. He chose the Argon model, noting that it was creative enough to write articles that are worth reading.

Users can also steer the generation in a choose‑your‑own‑adventure style when creating new articles. All content generated by Fakeipedia is free and publicly accessible.

The author welcomes suggestions for new world ideas and features that could improve the project. The post has received 8 points and 2 comments, and the comments can be viewed at https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50126334.
summary: Fakeipedia is an automatic world‑building platform that creates a clickable wiki for imagined worlds using the Argon AI model. It charges a $0.90 fee per generated article, and all content is free and public.

content:

title: Scientists find cell division reshapes tissues in crowded environments
content:
Scientists have uncovered a new function of cell division that extends beyond the creation of new cells, revealing that the process actively helps reshape tissues. This discovery addresses a fundamental biological challenge: how a tightly packed sheet of cells creates space for two daughter cells within an already crowded environment.

The research highlights the mechanical difficulties inherent in tissue growth and renewal, where cells must divide inside constrained spaces. By identifying this reshaping role, the study provides insight into the mechanics of how tissues expand and maintain their structure during development and regeneration.
summary: Scientists have discovered that cell division helps reshape tissues beyond just creating new cells. This process addresses how tightly packed cells make room for two daughter cells within a crowded environment.

title: New 3D Model Shows How Shadows Reshape Chemistry in Stellar Nurseries
content: A new high‑resolution 3D model has been released that explains how young stars reshape the clouds from which they form. The model, created by an international team led by Dr Brandt Gaches of the University of Duisburg‑Essen, shows that the uneven structure of stellar nurseries creates shadows that alter their chemistry. These chemical changes, in turn, influence the infrared emission observed by the James Webb Space Telescope. The study has been published in the journal Astronomy & Astrophysics.
summary: A new high‑resolution 3D model led by Dr Brandt Gaches from the University of Duisburg‑Essen shows how uneven structures in stellar nurseries create shadows that alter their chemistry and affect the infrared emission observed by the James Webb Space Telescope. content:

summary: Plants begin responding to spaceflight almost immediately after leaving Earth, according to a new University of Florida study. title: European rabbits now common in Britain, but once non-native invasive species
content:

title: Scientists discover gene controlling left- or right-coiling in Japanese snails
content:
Scientists have identified a gene that determines whether Japanese snails develop shells that coil to the left or to the right, offering new insights into the biological basis of handedness.  

The discovery was made by researchers from the University of Nottingham and Tohoku University, who studied wild Euhadra snails in Japan to understand what makes one snail a mirror image of another.
